title: The nine treasures
hookLine: remember Guru Tegh Bahadur and the nine treasures come running home

lines: HE LOST EVERYTHING THE WORLD TAKES.
cards: There's a strange thing in this line of the Ardas, and once you see it, it's hard to unsee. For a month we read Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks: the world is a dream, nothing stays, strength gone, all companions gone.

And we know how his life ended: arrested, imprisoned, executed in Delhi. By any ordinary measure, he lost everything the world can take. Yet when the Ardas reaches his name, it promises the opposite of loss.
Remember him, it says, and every kind of treasure comes running to your house. How does the man who lost everything become the one who brings everything home?

teach.b: The line is: tegh bahaadar simariai, ghar nau nidh aavai dhaai. Remember Tegh Bahadur, and the nine treasures come running home. Nau is nine.
Nidh is a treasure, a store of wealth. In old Indian lore, the nine treasures belonged to the god of riches: nine kinds of fabulous wealth, everything a person could want.
In ordinary use, nau nidh can stand for every good thing at once.
And notice the verb: aavai dhaai, comes running. Runs, like a child to the door.

teach.h: THE REAL TREASURE IS THE NAME.
teach.b: The Sukhmani Sahib, for one, says the nine treasures are the Name of God: whoever has the Name lacks nothing. So the promise in the Ardas works on two levels.

On the plain level, Sikhs ask that remembering the ninth Guru bring blessing to their homes. On the deeper level, it echoes his own saloks. The last one said: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it.
The man who lost everything the world can take was holding the one treasure it can't. Remember his name, too.

teach.h: TYAG MAL, BRAVE OF THE SWORD.
teach.b: He was born Tyag Mal; tradition says he was given the name Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword, after fighting bravely as a young man beside his father, Guru Hargobind.
Brave of the sword, and yet remembered for the treasure he held in his heart. That's the paradox the Ardas sets in one line: the poorest-looking moment, and the richest.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs say that remembering Guru Tegh Bahadur brings the nine treasures running home, and Gurbani often names the Name of God as the true nine treasures.

o: the nine treasures: every good thing, and the Name
nine coins placed before the Guru Granth Sahib
nine gifts given to a couple at a Sikh wedding

games.q: the nine treasures — tap the pairs.
p: a treasure, a store of wealth

s: in Gurbani, the real nine treasures are often said to be the Name
whoever has the Name lacks nothing.
Guru Tegh Bahadur was born with that name
tradition says he was born Tyag Mal and named Tegh Bahadur after showing bravery.
in the Ardas, the treasures trickle in slowly
aavai dhaai: they come running, like a child to the door.

games.q: the Ardas reaches the name of the Guru who lost everything the world can take. what does it promise?
o: that loss is coming for everyone.
that remembering him brings the nine treasures running home.
games.why: the man who held the Name, which nothing equals, is remembered as the one who brings every treasure home.

practice: Picture your home, or a home you love, and fill it slowly, not with money but with the treasures that would actually make it rich: a laugh at the dinner table, someone who listens, a quiet morning, a faith or a hope, a friend who drops by.
Name each one as it arrives, and notice which are already there. If you pray, say Waheguru, as the one treasure Gurbani says holds the rest.

wordCard.voice: Nau nidh, the nine treasures. Every good thing, and in Gurbani, the Name; remember the ninth Guru, and they come running home.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nau nidh, the nine treasures; every good thing, and in Gurbani, often the Name itself.

carryVoice: Your line: nine treasures home. The richest things in a house were never bought. Day six hundred eighteen, done.
